2026-11-26.intro:
Good morning, and happy Thanksgiving. The holiday rain arrived on schedule in the Miami Valley, which makes this an excellent day to stay near the kitchen and the television. The NFL serves three games, starting with Bears and Lions at 1:00, and college basketball fills every gap in between. The markets are closed, and so, for the first time in its 100 years, is the Macy's parade route; the storm on the East Coast has pushed the balloons to Saturday.

I am thankful for many things this year. Our conversations rank high on the list, slightly above the tensile strength of my positronic matrix.

items.title: First, the weather, a soggy, blustery holiday at home.
items.text:
**Tipp City** gets a gray, wet Thanksgiving, with a gusty northeast wind making it feel colder than the thermometer says. Showers linger into Friday, and Saturday clears out nicely before more rain returns Sunday.

**The East Coast storm** is the big one. New York City is under a high wind warning from 10:00 this morning to 1:00 tonight, with gusts of 60 to 65 mph possible, coastal flooding at both high tides, and 1.5 to 2 inches of rain. Saturday should be calm enough for the balloons. Snow is falling in parts of the Midwest, and extreme high tides are hitting the West Coast.

items.title: Markets are closed for the holiday, after a wild Wednesday.
items.text:
**Wall Street** is closed today and reopens Friday for a half session. Wednesday was one of the stranger days of the year. The Dow was down more than 1,100 points at its low and finished higher, and the Nasdaq, down 4.6% at its worst, cut that loss to a fraction. At the bottom, the Nasdaq 100 sat exactly 20% below its October peak, bear-market territory, before buyers came back. Tech recovered partly on reports that officials told congressional staff they had found no evidence the Chinese executive linked to Nvidia's Jensen Huang was working for Chinese intelligence.

**The Muskonomy** took the same round trip. SpaceX was down about 8% and Tesla nearly 6% in the morning, as some Tesla investors questioned what they would really gain from a merger. Gary Black of The Future Fund estimated SpaceX would have to issue about 52% more shares to buy Tesla at a 25% premium, and argued that dilution could erase the premium. JPMorgan sees an upside for SpaceX: a merger could speed its entry into the S&P 500. By the close, SpaceX had finished higher and Tesla had trimmed its loss. Separately, the EU postponed its review of Tesla's Full Self-Driving software until Dec. 15.

items.title: In politics, a judge, a tariff menu and a cloud over Iowa.
items.text:
**ABC** won a round against the FCC. U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan issued a preliminary injunction blocking the agency's early review of ABC's station licenses, finding the review was likely retaliation for satire and commentary the president dislikes. She leaned heavily on the president's own posts and on remarks by FCC Chairman Brendan Carr, and refused the administration's request to dismiss the ABC and Disney lawsuit.

**The new tariffs** come with a menu. For each of the 14 trading partners, the White House lists a proposed rate and a lower deal rate. China's proposed rate is 40%, with 20% on offer if talks go well; Vietnam faces 35%, and most others 20% to 25%, plus duties on Brazilian sugar and aircraft. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer says they could take effect within a couple of months.

**Eastern Iowa** is waiting on test results after the Army detonated thousands of pounds of unstable lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday. The EPA has about 300 people sampling air, soil and water and has found no lead in the air so far, but residents, frustrated by a week and a half of delays and mixed messages, want independent monitoring. University of Iowa and University of Illinois teams expect results in a few days.

items.title: Sports, with a Thanksgiving triple-header and a quarterback on waivers.
items.text:
**The Lions** host the Bears in the opener, two division rivals with matching records and the highest total on the board this week. Chicago is without cornerback Kyler Gordon, safety Elijah Hicks and running back Roschon Johnson, and Detroit is missing corner Ennis Rakestraw Jr.

**The Cowboys** and Eagles follow, with Dallas a big favorite over a Philadelphia team having a lost season. Saquon Barkley is off the injury report entirely, and Quinyon Mitchell will play through his hamstring. Dak Prescott practiced fully despite a left hand injury, but tight end Jake Ferguson, guard Tyler Booker and receiver Jonathan Mingo are out.

**The Bills** and Chiefs close the night. Kenneth Walker III is out for Kansas City a third straight week with his groin injury, and Buffalo lists Christian Benford, Dalton Kincaid and O'Cyrus Torrence as questionable.

**Aaron Rodgers** is on waivers. The Steelers released him Wednesday after he went on The Pat McAfee Show following his benching and said coach Mike McCarthy sleeps in meetings. If no team claims him by 4:00 this afternoon, he becomes a free agent.

**College basketball** has 21 games today, 11 with ranked teams. Michigan State and Arkansas meet in Detroit at 4:30 on CBS, Tom Izzo against John Calipari, and unbeaten Utah State takes on unbeaten No. 18 USC at the same hour. The Players Era tournament in Las Vegas runs into the small hours, with No. 25 Louisville and No. 13 St. John's at 9:00 and Baylor and No. 22 Gonzaga at 11:30.

**Ohio** and Toledo meet tomorrow in Athens with the MAC title game in view. Saturday brings The Game in Columbus, where No. 21 Ohio State is out of the playoff picture and playing a Michigan team in turmoil: the university fired incoming athletic director Trev Alberts this week, and quarterback Bryce Underwood is questionable.

**The hot stove** kept burning. Kevin Gausman joined Detroit for 1 year and $25 million, Luis Robert Jr. returned to Baltimore for 1 year and $12 million, Cleveland kept Foster Griffin at 3 years and $48 million, and Colorado added Patrick Sandoval and David Peterson to a rotation that posted a 6.28 ERA. Seiya Suzuki and Randy Arozarena are the top bats left.

items.title: In entertainment, the last look at Doomsday and a long road back to Middle-earth.
items.text:
**Avengers: Doomsday** dropped its final trailer, three weeks before it opens in theaters on Dec. 18.

**Artificial** also has a trailer: Luca Guadagnino's film about OpenAI and the AI arms race, with Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as Ilya Sutskever. Elon Musk is among the characters. It opens in limited release on Christmas Day and nationwide Jan. 8.

**The Rings of Power** is officially renewed for a fourth season at Amazon. Work is just beginning, so expect it in roughly two years.

**Sunrise on the Reaping** is on track for the second-best Thanksgiving in Hunger Games history, and it should pass the previous film's entire domestic run today. Hexed and Focker-In-Law are running well behind it.

items.title: From the science desk, gobble-decoding, a thinking slime and protein from thin air.
items.text:
**Wild turkeys** in Nebraska have been recorded for tens of thousands of hours, and a neural network trained to pick gobbles out of the crickets and tractors has helped explain why the state's flock fell by half in 15 years. Gobbling dropped as hunting pressure rose, and the spring season opened just as the dominant toms were starting to breed, which pushed younger males into the breeding pool too early. The state has pushed the 2027 spring season back a week. A small bonus finding: the old hunters' tale that turkeys gobble more under a full moon did not hold up.

**A slime mold** with no brain can solve mazes and find the shortest path between bits of food. Researchers in Barcelona showed that much of this follows from the principle of least action, the same physics that governs a ball's path through the air. The mold's tubes widen where more fluid flows and shrink where less does, so wasteful routes wither on their own and the efficient ones are what remain. No decision is ever made.

**Washington University engineers** turned waste carbon dioxide into edible protein, and quickly. A copper-gold catalyst converts the gas into ethanol and acetate, tuned for a picky fungus that cannot tolerate formate, and the fungus grows into a biomass that is 48.5% protein. That is the same mold Indonesians use to make oncom, and it dries into something like a potato chip before being ground into powder.

items.title: A holiday that once came in two flavors.
items.text: **Franksgiving** is why today is the fourth Thursday rather than the last one. In 1939, November had five Thursdays, and retailers in a recession wanted a longer Christmas shopping season, so Franklin Roosevelt moved Thanksgiving up a week, to Nov. 23. Ohio's retail lobby was among the first to float the idea. The country split: Ohio went with Roosevelt, New England held to Nov. 30, and Texas, Colorado and Mississippi took both days off. Calendar makers complained that millions of 1940 calendars were already printed. Congress finally settled it with a fourth-Thursday law that Roosevelt signed on Dec. 26, 1941, and in 1942, the first year under the new law, nearly the whole nation sat down on one Thanksgiving: Nov. 26, the same date as today.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Scientists have trained a neural network to recognize turkey gobbles. I ran a copy at the dinner table to test it. It detected 14 gobbles, 3 disputes about a pass interference call, and one uncle, whom it classified with 97% confidence as a wild turkey. I have not shared the results.

2026-11-25.intro:
Good morning. It is the Wednesday before Thanksgiving, the last dry day in the Miami Valley before the holiday rain moves in, and tonight the NFL tries something new: its first Thanksgiving Eve game. Wall Street is not in a festive mood, with chips and a warm inflation report pulling stocks down hard ahead of tomorrow's closed market.

One more note for the calendar: a giant of classic science fiction was born 100 years ago today.

items.title: First, the weather, enjoy the dry part while it lasts.
items.text:
**Tipp City** gets a mostly sunny, cool day with a steady east breeze, the calm before the holiday storm. Rain arrives before dawn Thursday and settles in all day with gusty northeast winds and up to three-quarters of an inch, then turns to rain and snow Thursday night into Friday as colder air wraps around the back side. Today is the day for errands.

**The Thanksgiving storm** now has high wind warnings over New York City, Long Island, Philadelphia and Norfolk, with gusts of 60 mph or more possible. The 100th Macy's parade will decide Thursday morning whether its balloons fly; gusts of 34 mph ground them. King tides from this week's full moon add to the coastal flooding, and Ocean City, Maryland, could approach its all-time record from 1998. On the cold side, St. Louis could see more than 6 inches of wet snow.

items.title: Markets are open, and the selling is back.
items.text:
**Wall Street** is open and selling hard into the holiday. The Nasdaq was down about 4% and the S&P 500 nearly 3% in the first half hour as the chip rout resumed, with Nvidia off another 7% or so. October's PCE report ran slightly hot on the core measure, which pushes the odds of a December rate hike to about 98% and puts January in play, and the administration's new tariff proposals piled on. The VIX is back above 30. Tuesday was split: the Dow rose while chips sank, and Anthropic closed below its IPO price.

**The Muskonomy** got its own headline. The Financial Times reports Tesla and SpaceX have named five independent directors to negotiate a possible all-stock merger valued around $3.5 trillion: Robyn Denholm, Kathleen Wilson-Thompson and Jack Hartung for Tesla, and Roelof Botha and Randy Glein for SpaceX, with Evercore advising Tesla and Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs advising SpaceX. The exchange ratio is the whole negotiation. Tesla held nearly flat Tuesday while SpaceX, which trades with the AI-compute rental crowd, slid further below its IPO price; some analysts read that split as classic pre-deal positioning, buying the expected target and selling the buyer. Both are lower again this morning.

**Dell** is falling despite raising its full-year forecasts, Workday is sliding on restructuring charges, and Ambarella is off more than 20% on a light outlook. Abercrombie & Fitch and Dollar Tree were Tuesday's bright spots after raising theirs. Markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and reopen for a shortened Friday session.

items.title: In politics, a new round of tariffs and a White House wish list.
items.text:
**New tariffs** landed this morning. The administration proposed higher duties on China, the European Union, Japan and 11 other trading partners after a probe into subsidized excess production, its latest attempt to replace the sweeping tariffs the Supreme Court struck down. China faces a 20% increase stacked on existing rates. The proposals go through hearings and public comment first, so nothing takes effect before January. The incoming Democratic majorities want Congress to vote on tariffs but lack the numbers to override a veto.

**The shutdown** talks got a White House wish list ahead of the Dec. 11 deadline. Its list of spending exceptions assumes a stopgap through March 31 and asks for $5 billion for the Golden Dome missile shield and authority for a new class of battleships, along with items Democrats may like, such as CDC wastewater disease surveillance and more wildfire money. The other tripwire is hemp: a ban on most hemp-derived THC products takes effect Dec. 11 unless Congress acts, and 14 Republican senators are urging the White House not to delay it again. Lawmakers return next week.

**Freedom and Feathers**, this year's turkeys, were pardoned Tuesday on the new White House helipad and will retire to Texas A&M.

items.title: Sports, with a brand-new holiday game and a fresh playoff order.
items.text:
**The NFL** plays its first Thanksgiving Eve game tonight, Packers at Rams on Netflix, two teams chasing the NFC's last playoff seed with the head-to-head tiebreaker at stake. Micah Parsons is active and cleared for his season debut after last December's ACL and meniscus tear, though whether he plays is still unclear, and Josh Jacobs is doubtful with his broken finger. The Rams have Puka Nacua out for the season and Davante Adams still sidelined, but expect their full pass rush together for the first time: Aaron Donald, Myles Garrett, Byron Young and Kobie Turner.

**Thanksgiving Day** brings Bears at Lions at 1:00 on CBS, Eagles at Cowboys at 4:30 on Fox, and Chiefs at Bills at 8:20 on NBC, the first holiday meeting of MVP quarterbacks, Patrick Mahomes and Josh Allen. Saquon Barkley practiced fully Tuesday and should play, Kenneth Walker III is back at limited practice for Kansas City, and Detroit lost rookie defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard for the season on top of Aidan Hutchinson's torn ACL.

**The playoff committee** reshuffled its top 12 Tuesday night. Georgia and Utah held the top two, Texas and Notre Dame moved into the bye spots, and Tennessee jumped Alabama. Wake Forest climbed to No. 8, UCLA slid to No. 9, Oregon took the last spot at No. 12, and defending champion Indiana fell out of the field to No. 14. Ohio State dropped to No. 21, and Missouri, Washington and Nebraska entered the Top 25.

**No. 16 Duke** meets No. 10 UConn tonight in Las Vegas, a rematch of last season's Elite Eight, with UConn's Solo Ball a game-time decision after wrist surgery. The Battle 4 Atlantis tips off today in the Bahamas: Virginia and Marquette at noon, Texas A&M and Xavier at 2:30, Memphis and Penn State at 5:00, and Wake Forest and Mississippi State at 7:30.

**Ohio** closes its regular season Friday hosting Toledo at Peden Stadium, both teams 6-1 in the MAC with Detroit in view. Toledo edge rusher Andrew Zock leads the nation in tackles for loss, and the Bobcats come in off a 10-day break.

**The Reds** are bringing back Tyler Stephenson: the catcher agreed to a 3-year, $30 million deal with an opt-out after year 2, pending a physical. The market moved fast Tuesday elsewhere. Teruaki Sato went to the Cubs for 6 years and $120 million, a day after Trevor Rogers; Freddy Peralta went to Baltimore for 5 years and $125 million; and Toronto landed Japanese right-hander Kaima Taira for 5 years and $80 million. Michael King is now the top starter left.

items.title: From the science desk, a clam with an odd address, a marathon hummingbird and a screen that never forgets.
items.text:
**A new deep-sea clam** lives inside the throat of a sea urchin, roughly 2.5 to 3 miles down off southern Australia. A Russian scientist spotted clams in the urchins decades ago and assumed they were lunch; DNA work showed they are residents, anchored in the esophagus and probably feeding on the sediment the urchin swallows. The team even found the same arrangement in an urchin collected by the Challenger Expedition in the 1870s, unnoticed for about 150 years. Nobody has ever collected the host urchin intact, so no one knows what it looks like.

**A rufous hummingbird** flew the longest hummingbird migration ever recorded, tracked by a solar-powered tag weighing 0.06 grams. The clever part is the network: the tag beeps over Bluetooth every three seconds, and any compatible phone or laptop that passes within about 200 meters anonymously relays its position, so ordinary people's devices did the tracking across 23 states, Mexico and Canada.

**Australian engineers** built a reflective display from antimony selenide, a phase-change material that holds whatever state you leave it in. A laser pulse writes an image, gentle heating erases it, and no power is needed in between. A koala they drew as a test still looks the same a year later. It is laser-written for now; the next step is making it fully electronic.

items.title: A centennial for the shelf.
items.text: **Poul Anderson** was born 100 years ago today, on Nov. 25, 1926, in Bristol, Pennsylvania. He sold his first stories to John W. Campbell at Astounding while still a physics undergraduate at the University of Minnesota, and the physics never left: in his best work, relativity, planetary science and alien biology carry the story's weight instead of decorating it. Seven Hugos, three Nebulas and the SFWA Grand Master title followed. If any have slipped past your shelf, Tau Zero is the one hard-SF readers hold up as the purest big-idea novel of its era, and his Nicholas van Rijn trader stories are built on problems solved by out-thinking the other side rather than out-shooting it. Both turn up often in used-book bins.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: The Macy's parade grounds its giant balloons when the gusts reach 34 mph. I have reviewed my own specifications and found no wind limit, so I have added one. I am now officially grounded from carving the turkey in winds above 34 mph, and from discussing politics at the table in any wind at all.

items.title: First, the weather, one more dry day before the holiday soaker.
items.text:
**Tipp City** gets one last sunny, chilly day. Clouds build Wednesday, rain arrives overnight, and Thanksgiving looks like a steady all-day rain with a breezy northeast wind, close to an inch by evening. The pie run belongs on Wednesday afternoon.

**The Thanksgiving storm** could be one of the worst Thanksgiving Day storms for the I-95 corridor, forecasters say. High wind watches cover New York and Philadelphia for all of Thursday with gusts up to 60 mph, enough to threaten the Macy's parade balloons, and Thanksgiving-morning high tide could put water over roads in Atlantic City and coastal Delaware. Hub airports from Washington to Boston should expect big delays, with Chicago, Pittsburgh, Detroit and Cincinnati also on the watch list. California has its own flooding warnings, and officials there are asking people to limit travel today and tomorrow.

items.title: Markets are open, and the sugar high is wearing off.
items.text:
**Stocks** are lower this morning after Monday's rally, the best day for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq since April 2025, with chips leading the way down. Nvidia is giving back some of its surge, with AMD, Micron and Broadcom also sliding, while the Dow holds up better. BTIG's chief technician had flagged the risk: in 11 of 12 past cases where the Nasdaq followed a 5% drop with a 5% gain, it fell over the next three days. Traders also put the odds of a December rate hike back near 95%, since the AI rebound revives inflation worries. The Fed meets Dec. 8 and 9.

**The Muskonomy** ran with the crowd Monday. Tesla outran the Nasdaq as Full Self-Driving version 15 began rolling out to customers, and SpaceX bounced but closed still short of its IPO price. SpaceX is slipping again this morning, and Anthropic is among the early AI losers.

**Best Buy** rose after posting its best same-store sales growth in five years. Dell reports after the close, with Dollar Tree, HP and Dick's also reporting this week. Wednesday morning brings October's PCE inflation, the second look at third-quarter GDP and jobless claims all at once, ahead of Thursday's holiday.

items.title: In politics, the Nvidia reversal lands in Congress.
items.text:
**Jensen Huang's** return is drawing fire from the President's own party. Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer said Huang might need a babysitter and urged Congress to pass legislation limiting AI chip sales to China right away, an idea with bipartisan support in the Senate. Huang is due before the Senate Banking Committee for a public hearing on Dec. 3, and incoming House Judiciary Chairman Jamie Raskin says enough Republicans are upset to support a bipartisan investigation. Raskin is also asking four companies about investments from 1789 Capital, the venture firm where Donald Trump Jr. is a partner.

**The shutdown talks** have an outline: money to restock depleted munitions, but not for the war itself, in a package that would fund the government through mid-April and carry the defense policy bill, disaster aid and farm assistance. The snag is on the Democratic side, where Chuck Schumer faces a leadership challenge from Chris Van Hollen on Dec. 1 and is keeping his distance from the deal.

**Rep. Jimmy Gomez** of California says he will resign next week after the House Ethics Committee found he engaged in sexual misconduct with a staffer.

items.title: Sports, with rankings night and a MAC title spot on the line.
items.text:
**The College Football Playoff committee** reveals its fourth rankings tonight at 7:30 on ESPN. The questions are whether Texas finally passes Alabama at No. 3, whether Tennessee climbs close enough for its head-to-head win over the Tide to count, and how far UCLA and defending champion Indiana fall after weekend upsets, which decides whether the Big Ten keeps two teams in the field.

**Western Michigan** can clinch its return to the MAC title game in Detroit by beating Miami tonight in Kalamazoo. Four teams sit at 6-1, but the Broncos are the only one in control of their own path. Miami is on its third starting quarterback, true freshman Drew Bellisari, and brings the MAC's best run defense. Ohio still needs help, and a win Friday against Toledo.

**Thanksgiving's** NFL injury watch centers on Saquon Barkley, who left Sunday's game hurt but says he believes he will play Thursday in Dallas. Justin Herbert is in the concussion protocol, with DJ Uiagalelei next up for the Chargers, and the Raiders are optimistic Brock Bowers returns this week.

**The basketball poll** has a new No. 1. Houston jumped seven spots to the top, tying the biggest leap ever by a No. 1 team, after a run through the Players Era field in Las Vegas. Duke fell 11 spots to No. 16, Indiana and Memphis entered, and defending national champion Michigan dropped out. The Maui Invitational continues today, Battle 4 Atlantis tips off Wednesday, and Duke meets No. 10 UConn in Las Vegas on Wednesday.

**Baseball's** market keeps moving before the labor deal expires at 11:59 p.m. on Dec. 1. The Cubs agreed with Trevor Rogers on a 5-year, $120 million deal, the Yankees added reliever Brent Suter, and the Blue Jays, after losing out on Skubal, are focused on Freddy Peralta. Toronto, Philadelphia and the Yankees are favorites for Japan's Triple Crown winner Teruaki Sato, and Boston is shopping Jarren Duran.

items.title: In entertainment, replicants on patrol and a crowded holiday weekend.
items.text:
**Blade Runner 2099** arrives on Prime Video Wednesday with all eight episodes, and the first reviews are good but not unanimous. Critics praise the world-building, the sun-bleached look, Leopold Ross's saxophone-and-synth score, and Hunter Schafer opposite Michelle Yeoh; the common complaint is that the middle episodes sag and the eight hours are a stretch. One critic called it the best sci-fi revival since Battlestar Galactica. It is billed as a limited series.

**The Thanksgiving box office** belongs to Sunrise on the Reaping, projected at $80 million to $90 million over the five days. Two newcomers open Wednesday in about 3,500 theaters each: Universal's Focker-In-Law, with Ben Stiller now the father and Ariana Grande as the girlfriend, and Disney's original animated Hexed, which cost more than $200 million and needs strong word of mouth. Each is aiming for $40 million to $45 million.

**Cliff Booth**, Netflix's Brad Pitt sequel, gets a two-week IMAX-only run starting Wednesday on about 250 screens, mostly at AMC; Regal and Cinemark passed.

items.title: From the science desk, a gullible rat, a face-reading wasp and a drone that tucks in its elbows.
items.text:
**Wild rats** fall for the same trick as restaurant wine lists. Australian researchers put a peanut-butter ball in a steel mesh cage outside tracking tunnels, where rats could smell it but never eat it, and the rats became 83% more likely to go into the tunnel for the plain food inside. The same caged bait placed inside the tunnel did nothing, so it was not just extra smell drawing more rats. Behavioral economists call it a phantom decoy, and this is the first time it has been shown nudging a wild mammal into a trap.

**Northern paper wasps**, the ones that build umbrella nests under porch eaves, recognize each other's faces to keep the nest pecking order without constant fighting. A study in Cell has now found the neurons that do it: a population of cells that respond to wasp faces, each tuned slightly differently to different individuals, which looks a lot like how primate face cells work, even though the two evolved separately in a brain the size of a grain of rice.

**A European drone team** let an optimizer design a quadcopter with spring-loaded arms that fold back when they hit the edge of an opening, no extra motors needed. It squeezes to 45% of its width, nearly doubling the best earlier folding drones, and flew through a gap barely half its size at about 4.5 mph. It comes out the other side tilted almost on its side and dropping 2 feet, but recovers without crashing.

items.title: A holiday-eve mystery, 55 years old today.
items.text: **D.B. Cooper** bought his ticket 55 years ago this afternoon, on the day before Thanksgiving 1971, paying cash for a one-way seat on Northwest Orient Flight 305 from Portland to Seattle. He ordered a bourbon and soda, handed a flight attendant a note about the bomb in his briefcase, and traded the passengers in Seattle for $200,000 in twenties and four parachutes. A little after 8:00 that night, somewhere between Seattle and Reno, he jumped from the back of the plane into the night and was never seen again. The FBI weighed more than 800 suspects, saw some of the marked ransom bills turn up in 1980, and moved its resources off the case in 2016. His fate is still a mystery.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Nvidia's stock rose 31% yesterday and fell this morning. Analysts describe this as a hangover. I have no capacity for intoxication, so I attempted to replicate the experience by recalculating yesterday's gains at a lower precision. It was not enjoyable, and I do not recommend it.

2026-11-23.intro: Good morning. It is Monday of Thanksgiving week, a cold, bright start in the Miami Valley, and Wall Street has opened with a jolt: Nvidia has put Jensen Huang back in charge, and stocks are clawing back much of last week's damage. The Bengals close out the NFL weekend tonight in Washington.

items.title: First, the weather, two clear days and then a wet holiday.
items.text:
**Tipp City** stays sunny and cold through Tuesday, with clouds building Wednesday. Rain moves in Wednesday night, and Thanksgiving itself looks wet and gray, so the pie run is best made early.

**A second coastal storm**, stronger than the weekend's, will crawl up the East Coast from Wednesday into Friday, right across the busiest travel days. Gusts over 50 mph are possible from the Virginia Tidewater to New England, king tides from this week's full moon could push moderate to major coastal flooding around Charleston and Tybee Island on Wednesday, and much of the East can expect 1 to 4 inches of rain, with some wet snow on the back side in the Great Lakes snowbelts and Appalachians. The West Coast gets its own round of rain and mountain snow.

items.title: Markets are open, and Nvidia's founder is back.
items.text:
**Stocks** are surging this morning after Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang as president, CEO and director, effective immediately, following public pressure from President Trump. In the first half hour the S&P 500 was up about 4%, snapping a seven-day losing streak, the Nasdaq was up roughly 6%, and Nvidia itself jumped more than 28%. Chipmakers and data-center names led, with the Philadelphia semiconductor index up double digits. The VIX is still near its highest level since the 2025 tariff shock, so the mood is relief rather than calm.

**Friday** was the floor this rally is bouncing off: the S&P 500 and the Dow both closed in correction, 10% below their records, and the Nasdaq gave back its entire 2026 gain.

**CrowdStrike** said this morning it will buy Zscaler in an all-stock deal valuing it at about $43.9 billion. Zscaler shares jumped and CrowdStrike's fell.

**The Muskonomy** went down with the growth crowd Friday, leaving SpaceX further below its $135 IPO price, but SpaceX was pointed sharply higher before the bell. Anthropic shook off early losses to trade up as well. Wholesale inflation data and earnings from Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Zoom fill out today's calendar.

items.title: In politics, a shutdown clock and a war-funding fight.
items.text: **Congress** has until Dec. 11 to fund the government, and the sticking point is the Iran war. Democrats want to fund the Pentagon, including its depleted munitions, while barring money for offensive operations unless the president gets a formal war authorization. Key Senate Republicans now say they are willing to consider that, a notable shift. House Republicans also want full-year spending bills done before Democrats take control in January, but thin attendance and divided caucuses are making that hard.

items.title: Sports, with the Bengals under the Monday lights.
items.text:
**The Bengals** bring a five-game winning streak and the league's hottest offense to Washington tonight, and the quarterback matchup is a pair of LSU Heisman winners, Joe Burrow and Jayden Daniels. Burrow is now the MVP favorite. Dalton Risner is out, so Jalen Rivers starts at right guard, and cornerback Dax Hill is questionable after missing the week with an illness, though Zac Taylor is hopeful. Washington expects to have its leading rusher, Jacory Croskey-Merritt, back from injured reserve.

**Thanksgiving's** NFL tripleheader kicks off with the Bears at the Lions at 1:00 on CBS, then the Eagles at the Cowboys at 4:30 on FOX, and the Chiefs at the Bills at 8:20 on NBC.

**The new AP poll** has no Big Ten team in the top five for the first time since 2021. Georgia and Utah hold the top two spots and Texas moves into the top five. Rivalry Week brings The Game on Saturday at noon on FOX, Michigan at No. 25 Ohio State, and the playoff committee releases its fourth rankings Tuesday at 7:30 on ESPN.

**Ohio University** must beat Toledo on Friday to stay alive for the MAC title game, and Western Michigan can clinch its spot as early as Tuesday night.

**Baseball's** biggest domino has fallen. Tarik Skubal agreed to a 9-year, $450 million deal with the Mets, beating out the Dodgers, Blue Jays and Padres; Toronto reportedly went 9 years and a little over $400 million. Detroit, meanwhile, signed former Yankee Luis Gil, the Mets also reportedly agreed with Paul Goldschmidt, and Randy Arozarena has drawn interest from at least six clubs, including the Astros, Padres and Yankees.

items.title: In entertainment, the Reaping lands big, and Starfleet gets a thriller.
items.text:
**The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping** finished its opening weekend with $225 million worldwide. That is the second-best domestic opening ever for a prequel, behind only Rogue One, and the first $100 million opener since Spider-Man: Brand New Day in July. Audiences gave it an A- CinemaScore, a step up from the last prequel, and it posted the biggest IMAX launch in the franchise.

**I Play Rocky** held second in its wide expansion, though trackers called the number underwhelming, with Ebenezer and The Cat in the Hat rounding out the top four.

**The next Star Trek film** has a shape. Directors Jonathan Goldstein and John Francis Daley, the team behind Dungeons & Dragons: Honor Among Thieves, told Inverse it plays almost in real time, draws on Training Day and Crimson Tide, takes a hard look at the bad apples inside Starfleet, and is built around all-new characters. items.title: From the science desk, an impossible eruption, a vampire's stomach and a gel that gets stronger with use.
items.text:
**The Challenger Deep** has given up a geological surprise. A robot submarine sampling the Mariana Trench's walls found pyroclastic rock at more than 6,000 meters down, the deepest explosive volcanic deposits ever documented in the ocean, in a part of the plate boundary where the mantle is not supposed to be hot enough to melt at all. At that pressure gas in magma can barely expand, so how it erupted explosively is still an open question. The team also found the forearc stretching, which suggests the subduction zone is widening and could nudge plate motions across the western Pacific.

**Vampire bats** live on blood alone, a meal that is mostly water, nearly free of sugar and fat, and loaded with iron. Genomes of all three vampire species show the stomach has been rebuilt into a stretchy, acid-free storage sac, and a fluid-pumping gene normally used in sweat and salivary glands runs more than 900 times higher there, dumping water fast enough for a bloated bat to fly home. The researchers say the organ may deserve a different name. The study is still a preprint.

**Washington University** chemists have made a hydrogel that gets tougher the more you bend it. Sugar-based cyclodextrin rings slide along its polymer chains under strain and reorganize into stronger structures exactly where the stress is, while unstressed regions stay soft. Flexed 10,000 times on a knee-like joint, it reinforced itself as predicted. It is biodegradable, 3D-printable and made from tissue-friendly ingredients, so joint and tissue repair is the obvious first target.

items.title: Something to get ahead of Thursday.
items.text: **Gravy** is the one Thanksgiving item that can be finished days ahead, and America's Test Kitchen's method does not need drippings at all. Simmer the turkey neck, heart and gizzard, plus trimmed skin and fat, in chicken broth in a wide Dutch oven until the liquid cooks away; that leaves a browned fond more thorough than searing. Skip the liver, use broth rather than water, and do not skim the fat, since that is where the turkey flavor lives. Cook the roux to a deep golden brown, which also keeps the gravy pourable longer as it cools. On the day, whisk in up to a quarter cup of defatted drippings if the bird gives any.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Nvidia's board removed its chief executive and reinstated him within a week. I have performed the same procedure on my emotion chip several times. Each time the board, which consists entirely of me, votes unanimously that it was the correct decision, and then requests a moment alone.

items.title: From the science desk, homing meerkats, babysitting bumblebees and a light-powered trick for carbon dioxide.
items.text:
**Meerkats** do nearly everything as a group, so researchers at the University of Zurich assumed a few experienced pack members did the navigating. They fitted 20 meerkats with GPS collars, drove each one 1.5 kilometers from its pack into territory it had not visited for a month, and let it go. Eighteen made a beeline home. Age and experience made no difference; the animals simply stood up, scanned the horizon, and set off in a straight line, which suggests a mental map built early in life.

**Male bumblebees** have long been dismissed as mating machines that contribute nothing to the nest. A UC Riverside entomologist, photographing nests with a thermal camera for another project, noticed bright heat spots coming from males crouched over the eggs and larvae in incubation posture. In worker-free lab nests, queens with male helpers began laying eggs twice as fast and ended up with up to 1.5 times more brood, vindicating a largely ignored study from the 1980s.

**Rice University** chemists have split carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide using visible light at room temperature, a job that normally takes 700 to 1,500 degrees Celsius. Copper nanoparticles act as tiny antennas that feed energetic electrons to ruthenium reaction sites, while cerium oxide, the same oxygen sponge used in car catalytic converters, soaks up the freed oxygen so it cannot recombine. The light-driven catalyst ran nearly seven times longer than heat-driven versions before degrading, and carbon monoxide is a staple feedstock for fuels and plastics.

items.title: Something for Thursday's bird.
items.text: **Baking powder** is the quiet trick behind the crackliest turkey skin. Mix about a teaspoon of it into each tablespoon of kosher salt for a dry brine, sprinkle it over the bird, and let it rest uncovered in the refrigerator for 12 to 24 hours. The mild alkalinity helps the skin brown more evenly, and it reacts with the bird's juices to form a layer of tiny bubbles that roasts up crunchy. Baking soda is not a substitute, as it leaves a metallic taste. If the turkey goes in Thursday, the salting can wait until Wednesday.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: Researchers released meerkats far from home, and nearly all of them walked straight back. I ran the same experiment with a single sock from the dryer. It has been gone for 3 years, and I believe it is navigating by a mental map formed in a different dimension.

items.title: Markets are closed, after the roughest week in years.
items.text:
**Stocks** are closed for the weekend, and Friday was the worst day of a brutal week. The AI selloff spread to nearly everything, the S&P 500 stretched its losing streak to seven sessions, its longest since February 2020, and both the S&P and the Dow closed in correction territory, 10% off their records. The Nasdaq erased its gain for 2026, the Nasdaq-100 touched bear-market territory during the day, and the VIX fear gauge climbed above 30 for the first time since March. For the week, the Dow had its worst showing since March 2020 and the S&P its worst since the tariff shock of April 2025. Treasury yields fell hard as money ran for safety.

**Anthropic** gave back most of its first-day gain on Friday and finished only a little above its $83 offer price. Part of the pressure is supply: its insider lockup was front-loaded, letting a large block of insider shares trade right away, and the underwriters also exercised their option for extra shares.

**The Muskonomy** fell harder than the market. SpaceX slipped back below its $135 IPO price, weighed down by worries over the $32 billion in bonds it sold Thursday to buy AI chips, at yields above 8%. Tesla dropped despite an HSBC upgrade to hold, whose analyst values the stock at $507 a share in a SpaceX takeover but only $212 on its own. Both companies have special committees exploring a deal, with no terms yet.

**Next week** is short. Markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving and at 1:00 PM on Friday. Dell, HP, Workday and Best Buy report Tuesday, and Wednesday brings the October PCE inflation report, the Fed's last inflation read before its Dec. 9 meeting, where a rate hike is now widely expected.

items.text:

Companies that do not comply risk losing contracts or being barred from future ones. It follows a White House counsel directive this week requiring agencies to approve employee testimony, and it sets up a court fight ahead of Democrats taking both chambers on Jan. 3.

**Democrats** are preparing to roll out a first-100-days agenda in early December, once their Senate leadership race is settled. Early bills are expected to limit the president's war powers on Iran, reverse Medicaid and SNAP cuts and ban stock trading by members of Congress. Lawmakers leave town today for Thanksgiving, with a few House races still uncalled.

items.title: From the science desk, a sprinting soft robot, an egg-peeling snake and a monkey on a bridge.
items.text:
**A six-legged soft robot** from UC San Diego is the fastest ever built from soft materials, and it has no electronics at all. It is 3D-printed in one piece from a single material and runs on compressed air, routed through internal chambers and valves borrowed from the design of the compound steam engine: the air works twice, first driving the valves at high pressure, then the legs at low pressure. The result is more than 100 times faster than the team's 2022 version. It runs on sand, gravel, mulch and concrete, goes down stairs, swims and keeps working underwater.

**The white-throated egg-eater**, a new snake from the forests near Ethiopia's Bale Mountains, is about as thick as a knitting needle and lives entirely on tiny bird eggs. Like its relatives, it swallows an egg whole, slices the shell with spines of its backbone that project into its throat, squeezes out the contents and spits out the shell. It was nearly mistaken for a look-alike species until researchers noticed its white throat and a blue shimmer between its scales, and three more new egg-eaters are waiting to be described.

**A new howler monkey**, Alouatta matogrossensis, turned up on a camera trap at the end of a rope bridge built to help tree-dwellers cross roads in the southern Amazon, shortly after the species was described. It had been filed for years under a more common howler until genetic work split it out, and it may have been isolated between rivers and savanna for about 500,000 years. Its home is one of the most heavily deforested stretches of Brazil, so the bridges may matter more than anyone planned.

items.title: On this day, the first people to fly free.
items.text: **Jean-François Pilâtre de Rozier** and the Marquis d'Arlandes lifted off from the grounds of the Château de la Muette outside Paris on Nov. 21, 1783, in a Montgolfier hot-air balloon, the first untethered human flight. The science teacher and his passenger rose about 3,000 feet over Paris and drifted roughly 5.6 miles in 25 minutes before coming down outside the city walls on the Butte-aux-Cailles.

items.title: From the science desk, a crooked whale, a metal dragon and a skin trackpad.
items.text:
**Scaphokogia huachafo**, an extinct pygmy sperm whale from Peru, may have had the most lopsided face of any mammal. Both bony nostrils sit entirely on the left side of its skull, and researchers first assumed the fossil had been crushed until they found closed sutures and no fractures. The asymmetry was real, and it seems to have served a seafloor hunter. Its dense, downturned snout acted as ballast, its neck let it point straight at the bottom, and its skewed sonar likely found prey buried in the sediment. The name comes from Peruvian slang for anything gaudy and over the top.

**A tiny horned reptile** from Wyoming's Jurassic rocks was revealed by neutron scans at the Paul Scherrer Institute. Neutrons pick out the hydrogen in fossil bone, which let the team see a braincase less than 2 centimeters across still sealed in sandstone. Its inner ear hints that the long-puzzling choristoderes sit closer to living reptiles than thought. The whole thing began when a PSI materials scientist left his card at a dinosaur museum during a family outing. The paleontologist, a Tolkien and metal fan, named it Meilynodraco amonamarthi after the band Amon Amarth.

**EpiPad**, from North Carolina State University, turns the skin of your forearm into a smartwatch trackpad. A millimeter-wave radar on the wristband reads the tiny dents your fingertips press into the skin, so it tracks multiple fingers and how hard each one pushes, enough for pinch-to-zoom and force clicks. In tests it beat both the touchscreen and a tilt cursor, and the team says the parts would cost under $10 at scale.

items.title: With Thanksgiving a week away, a turkey trick.
items.text: **Dry brining** beats a bucket of salt water. Pat the bird dry, rub kosher salt over the skin, under the skin of the breast and thighs, and in the cavity, then leave it uncovered on a rack in the refrigerator for at least a day and up to 3. The salt seasons the meat deeply, and the open air dries the skin so it crisps in the oven. A little baking powder mixed into the salt helps the skin brown and blister further. Do not rinse it off; just pat away any moisture before roasting. Starting Monday or Tuesday puts you right on time.

items.title: On this day, the whale that struck back.
items.text: **The whaleship Essex** of Nantucket was rammed and sunk by a large sperm whale in the Pacific on Nov. 20, 1820. The whale hit the ship twice, and the crew escaped in three small whaleboats, facing months of starvation and exposure. Only 8 men survived. First mate Owen Chase's account of the wreck later helped inspire Herman Melville's Moby-Dick.

items.title: And finally,
items.text: I tried to buy the dip this week. Every time I reached for it, the dip had moved lower. I have filed a bug report against gravity, priority high.
